BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Behind this system, the synoptic pattern amplifies substantially heading into early next week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Near to slightly above normal temperatures through Friday.
- A weak cold front brings a slight chance of showers to Baker County and the West Central Mountains of Idaho on Sunday.
- Significantly above normal temperatures develops next week, peaking Wednesday around 15 degrees above normal with potential record highs.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Quiet and dry weather is expected across southeast Oregon and southwest Idaho through Saturday night. An upper level ridge builds into the Intermountain West behind departing weak northwest flow, allowing heights and thickness values to steadily rise. Dry air will maintain mostly clear to partly cloudy skies with light surface winds, though some overnight valley inversions and patchy early morning fog remain possible in sheltered basins. High temperatures will trend upward each afternoon, climbing several degrees above normal for early November. Lows will remain seasonal to slightly mild. No significant weather hazards or travel impacts are anticipated through the period.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: A weak shortwave and accompanying cold front will track across the Pacific Northwest on Sunday. Moisture and dynamics remain quite limited with this boundary, confining a slight chance of light showers mainly to northern Baker County and the West Central Mountains of Idaho. The remainder of southwest Idaho and southeast Oregon will stay dry with little more than passing mid and high clouds.

Behind this system, the synoptic pattern amplifies substantially heading into early next week. A deep upper level trough establishes itself off the Pacific Coast, pumping strong south- southwesterly flow and anomalous warmth northward into the Great Basin and northern Intermountain region. Temperatures will climb rapidly from Monday onward. By Wednesday, high temperatures are projected to peak in the mid to upper 60s for lower elevation valleys, which is roughly 15 degrees above seasonal normals. Several locations, including the Treasure Valley, could approach or exceed daily record highs. Dry and tranquil conditions will persist across the forecast area through mid-week under this strong ridge before model guidance begins to hint at unsettled weather approaching late in the week as the offshore trough edges eastward.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: The Intermountain West will see a ridge develop over the region on Saturday that will stick around in some form through next work week. The ensemble data shows almost no chance for precipitation in our CWA until the weekend of November 14-15.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Very light mountain snow possible on Friday in the high country with snow amounts less than 1".
- Pleasant temperatures and dry conditions are expected Saturday through late next week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: There is a ridge over Colorado with very light flow within it. The subsidence has created a pleasant day with temperatures in the upper 50s to low 60s across the plains with plenty of sunshine.

The current water vapor imagery shows an elongated trough extending from northwest Montana to California. Models had recently been showing this trough producing enough lift to generate snow showers over the mountains tomorrow afternoon and evening. However, the latest model runs split this trough with a piece staying over North Dakota and another piece moving to Arizona tomorrow. In the middle, over Colorado, there will be minimal lift and limited moisture. The question is now, will there be any snow showers at all? Compared to the question of, how much snow will fall? The forecast was edited to show a 20-30% chance of snow shows in the mountains tomorrow with other locations remaining dry. Snow amounts will be less than 1" and most locations won't see any accumulation at all.

The Intermountain West will see a ridge develop over the region on Saturday that will stick around in some form through next work week. The ensemble data shows almost no chance for precipitation in our CWA until the weekend of November 14-15. There will be very pleasant temperatures with highs slowly warming from the low 60s to close to 70 later in the week across the plains. With light winds, no critical fire weather conditions are expected so there will be no impactful weather.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Wednesday-Thursday...Ridging aloft reasserts itself across the Great Basin States from western Montana to Utah, keeping our counties in northerly flow aloft.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Near average temperatures and mostly dry conditions are expected through the remainder of the work week.
- Warmer temperatures are likely to return this weekend with dry weather conditions continuing.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: The clouds have cleared out for a rather sunny afternoon for the Southeast Wyoming and Western Nebraska Panhandle area. Temperature remained about normal for the forecast area with temperatures in the mid 50's for the lower elevations and the mid 40's for the higher elevations. The clouds will start to push back in this evening and into the overnight period ahead of a weak shortwave pushing through the Intermountain West. For the most part their may be a light drizzle for the mountain peaks tomorrow afternoon, but the rest of the forecast area is expected to remain dry. By Friday, afternoon we should start to see the cloud cover start to break up and the sun start to poke through. However, the high temperatures tomorrow should be relatively the same as today plus or minus a couple degrees. However, Friday night will be a little colder as clear skies are expected overnight. Overnight temperatures may drop a little colder than forecasted especially in our colder areas like Alliance, Douglas, and Laramie who seem to radiationally cool faster and more efficiently that the rest of the region. Those areas may experience overnight temperatures into the low 20's depending on when the skies clear over those areas.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Saturday...Ridging aloft bulges across Wyoming, helping to produce surface lee troughing and a warming trend. Continued dry with a lack of low and mid level moisture.
Sunday...Well pronounced ridging aloft continues, keeping us mild and dry. 700 mb temperatures near 6 Celsius will yield maximum temperatures from the upper 50s to upper 60s.
Monday-Tuesday...Dry and mild weather will continue with westerly flow aloft and only a weak positively tilted shortwave trough aloft moving across Wyoming on Tuesday.

Wednesday-Thursday...Ridging aloft reasserts itself across the Great Basin States from western Montana to Utah, keeping our counties in northerly flow aloft. 700 mb temperatures from 0 to 2 Celsius will help produce high temperatures from the mid 50s to mid 60s.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: A quick, transitory ridge will build over the area today though some high clouds will start infiltrating the region from west to east ahead of the next shortwave.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A few rivers and waterways across southeast Utah are still elevated due to runoff. Flood Warnings remain in effect for those areas.
- A quick system moves through tomorrow possibly bringing an isolated shower or two to the higher terrain.
- Warmer and drier conditions highlight the remainder of the seven-day forecast.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A quick, transitory ridge will build over the area today though some high clouds will start infiltrating the region from west to east ahead of the next shortwave. As the wave moves through on Friday, some very isolated showers may occur over the higher terrain with maybe some light snow at the highest elevations. Do not anticipate any accumulations, maybe a light dusting, as the wave moves through. As we head towards the evening hours, clouds will lift from west to east. After that, high pressure builds back in Sunday and persists for much of next week. High temperatures will start inching up above seasonal norms next week. This will be welcome relief after all the rain and unsettled weather we've seen recently.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: From Saturday into late week, confidence is high that dry weather will continue. A weak wave which was previously to affect parts of the region on Saturday now appears it will drop too far south, and we will not see any sensible weather with this system.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Quiet weather expected during this forecast period.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: A quiet weather pattern is expected during this forecast period. Although we will see a few weak disturbance move through during this period (especially tomorrow and mid week), these disturbances are quite dry and no impactful weather is expected with the disturbances.

for the rest of today through tomorrow, it will be dry. Max temps tomorrow will cool off a few degrees from todays max temps, with readings in the 50s to around 60F plains, and 40s larger valleys. We may see a few more higher clouds tomorrow across the region.
Mins tonight will be around freezing on the plains with 20s valleys. Temps will be 2-3 F warmer Saturday morning across the region.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: From Saturday into late week, confidence is high that dry weather will continue. A weak wave which was previously to affect parts of the region on Saturday now appears it will drop too far south, and we will not see any sensible weather with this system. Overall, max temps during this period will be running about 5 to 10F above normal for this time of the year, with max temps generally in the 60s plains and 50s larger valleys. \/Hodanish

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Models show fairly good consensus in precipitation chances not really increasing until around Thursday next week at the earliest.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Widely isolated showers possible late Thursday afternoon into the evening across northern Utah and southwest Wyoming with a weak system. Best chances noted in high terrain.

- Modestly strong wind gusts around 25-45 mph will develop across portions of Washington County Friday morning to evening, primarily in the Pine Valley Mountains area and favorably oriented canyons such as Black Ridge Canyon.
- A stretch of more mild and dry weather is expected Friday into the middle of next week or so as ridging becomes the dominant influence.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A seasonably cool start to the morning across the region, with some patchy fog noted in places such as the Uinta Basin, Cache Valley, Bear River Valley, and other some other sheltered mountain valleys. This will continue to lift and scatter out as the day progresses. Mid to upper level cloud cover is also gradually increasing as a shortwave trough continues to move in. Moisture with this feature is pretty limited overall, but high resolution models do at least carry a low end chance at some isolated showers from around mid afternoon to evening for portions of northern Utah to southwest Wyoming. The best chances are noted across the higher terrain, especially the Uintas. Would also not entirely rule out some patchy fog development late night into the morning again in similar areas that saw fog development this morning.

Impacts wise, the only thing of note with this system is some development of modest wind gusts around 25-45 mph across portions of the Pine Valley Mountains and gaps into favorably SW to NE oriented canyons (such as Black Ridge) as the trough sinks deeper into the Four Corners region. These look to increase by Friday morning, become maximized late Friday evening, and finally decrease through the overnight hours.

Overall, ridging gradually becomes the dominant forecast influence moving towards the weekend and on into the upcoming week. This will allow for a period of drier and more stable weather, with temperatures gradually warming back to above seasonal normal. A few grazing systems look to bring periods of increased cloud cover, but precipitation chances will remain very low.

Models show fairly good consensus in precipitation chances not really increasing until around Thursday next week at the earliest. Even then, there is a good deal of spread in those details of how any such potential system moves in, how much moisture accompanies it, and how long any unsettled period would last. Still, at least there remains a favorable signal for something in that extended range.

2660.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Chris Dickson
bottom_line: Avalanche danger is easing as the snowpack settles under calm, clear weather. The most dangerous slopes are where recent winds drifted snow into thicker, stiffer slabs on steep slopes above 12,000 feet facing northwest to north through east. Below 12,000 feet, the snowpack remains shallow.
Look for and avoid pockets of wind-buffed snow and pillowy drifts in cross-loaded couloirs, rocky windward slopes, and lee slopes directly below ridgelines.

2745.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Andrew McWilliams
bottom_line: Most slopes lack enough snow to produce an avalanche. Steer around steep slopes near ridgelines with continuous, firm snow cover. You might find these slopes at high elevations.

2842.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Andrew McWilliams
bottom_line: New snow on Wednesday night means you might find a fresh drift and trigger a small avalanche above treeline on Friday. Look for and avoid drifts in leeward catchments, like just below ridgelines, and along gully walls. Because wind speeds with this storm are light, the drifted snow may be softer and less obvious than the typical Colorado wind slab. Most slopes near and below treeline lack enough snow to produce an avalanche.
